Read About Amman

A city built on seven hills that has spent three thousand years being conquered, renamed, abandoned, and rebuilt — and the last fifty years absorbing more refugees than almost any capital on Earth.

A capital that keeps starting over

Amman does not look like a city with an ancient past. Drive in from Queen Alia International Airport and what you see first is limestone apartment blocks climbing hillside after hillside, a skyline with almost no landmark taller than a mosque minaret, a city that reads as thoroughly modern. The ancient part is there, but it hides in plain sight, up on the hill above downtown, where the Citadel has watched over one settlement after another since the Bronze Age.

The Ammonites built a city here they called Rabbath Ammon. The Ptolemies renamed it Philadelphia, after Ptolemy II Philadelphus, and it became one of the ten cities of the Roman Decapolis — the reason a 6,000-seat Roman theater still sits carved into a hillside in the middle of downtown. The Byzantines built churches on the Citadel. The Umayyads, ruling from Damascus in the seventh and eighth centuries, built a palace complex up there too, its distinctive domed audience hall still standing. Then, for reasons historians still debate — a devastating earthquake in 749 CE is the leading suspect — the city emptied out. For roughly a thousand years, Amman was a village, sometimes not even that.

What rebuilt it was not local growth but two waves of arrival a century apart. In 1878, the Ottoman government resettled Circassian refugees — Muslims driven from the Caucasus by Russian expansion — in the ruins of the old Roman city, and their descendants still form a distinct community in Amman today. Then in 1921, the British installed Emir Abdullah I as ruler of the newly created Emirate of Transjordan, and he chose this rebuilt village of a few thousand people as his capital, mostly because it sat on the Hejaz Railway line to Damascus. Neither choice looked obviously destined for greatness. Amman became a capital by accident of geography and colonial administration, not because anyone planned a great city here.

The city that never stops absorbing

What actually built modern Amman was refugees, in wave after wave, most of them not by choice. The 1948 and 1967 wars with Israel sent hundreds of thousands of Palestinians across the river; many settled permanently, and Ammanis of Palestinian origin are now a substantial share of the population. The 1990 Gulf War displaced Jordanian and Palestinian workers from Kuwait back to Amman. The 2003 Iraq War brought a wave of Iraqi arrivals, some wealthy enough to reshape entire neighborhoods of West Amman with their spending. The Syrian civil war after 2011 brought the largest wave yet, pushing the city's population past four million and straining water, housing, and traffic in ways still visible today.

A city built on seven hills has become a city of nearly twenty. Amman's growth was never zoned or planned from a single center — it spread hill by hill, wave by wave, and the numbered traffic circles that structure how Ammanis give directions are themselves a record of the city's outward creep from the old downtown.

This is the fact that explains almost everything else about how Amman feels to a visitor: it is a capital shaped less by kings and monuments than by the accumulated weight of people who arrived because home became impossible, and stayed because Amman, whatever its faults, let them build a life. Ask an Amman taxi driver where their family is from and the answer is rarely "Amman." It is usually Nablus, or Hebron, or Damascus, or Baghdad, or a village that may no longer exist. The city's cosmopolitanism was not curated. It was assembled under pressure, generation after generation, and it shows in the food, in the accents, in the sheer range of what "Jordanian" has come to mean.

Why every building is the same color

The other thing a visitor notices immediately is the limestone. Almost every building in Amman, from a 1930s downtown shopfront to a glass-fronted bank tower in Abdali, is clad in the same pale local stone. This is not an aesthetic accident — it has been a building code since the early twentieth century, when the city's planners required white or cream limestone facing on new construction, partly for the way it reflects the fierce summer sun and partly to give a fast-growing, architecturally chaotic city some visual coherence. The result is a skyline that can look monotonous from a distance and genuinely beautiful at sunset, when the whole hillside turns gold at once.

The limestone rule is also why the Citadel matters so much to how the city understands itself. From up there, looking out over the honey-colored hills in every direction, Amman reads less as a collection of separate neighborhoods and more as one continuous material — proof that whatever else divides the city's Circassian, Palestinian, Iraqi, Syrian, and East Bank Jordanian communities, they have all, quite literally, been built from the same stone.

Downtown versus the west side

Amman's clearest internal divide is not really about ethnicity but about elevation and era. Downtown — the valley around the Roman Theater and the old souks — is the oldest part of the modern city: dense, loud, unglamorous, full of the falafel counters and gold shops that have operated for generations. Rainbow Street and Jabal Amman, just up the hill, were the city's first fashionable expansion in the mid-twentieth century, and they still carry that slightly faded, high-ceilinged elegance in their 1920s and '30s townhouses, now converted into cafés and galleries.

Keep heading west, though, and the city changes generation by generation: Shmeisani's 1970s office blocks, then the newer glass towers of Abdali, built on the site of the old central bus station and meant to be a Gulf-style downtown of its own, then the sprawling villas of Abdoun and Dabouq further out still, where the diplomatic corps and the wealthiest Iraqi and Syrian arrivals settled. Driving west across Amman is, in a real sense, driving forward through the decades of who arrived and when, and what they could afford to build once they got here.

What the numbered circles are actually for

Ask for directions in Amman and you will be told a circle number before you are told a street name — First Circle, Third Circle, Sixth Circle — because the numbered roundabouts along Zahran Street were, for most of the twentieth century, the only fixed reference points as the city expanded westward with no consistent street-naming system behind it. Locals still navigate by circle and by landmark rather than by address, which is why a hotel address in Amman is more likely to read "near Fourth Circle" than a street number. It is a small, practical trace of a city that grew faster than its own bureaucracy could keep up with — and, like the limestone, it is one more way Amman's physical layout tells you the story of how it got built.
